Lawful
law'ful
a. (permitted by law; allowable; rendering Greek exesti, it is permitted)
From law, Saxon lagu, and the suffix -ful. The Greek behind most New Testament uses is the impersonal exesti, it is lawful or it is permitted — a word about permission rather than about obligation.

Biblical Definition

Lawful asks what is permitted, and Scripture repeatedly shows that it is not the last question. The Pharisees make it their first: “Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day” (Matthew 12:2), of men plucking ears of corn as they walked. Our Lord answers with David eating the shewbread and priests profaning the sabbath blamelessly, and then puts his own question, which reframes the whole category: “Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?” (Mark 3:4) — and the text notes that they held their peace, because the question could not be answered without abandoning their position. Paul takes up the word twice with the same qualification: “All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any” (1 Corinthians 6:12). He grants the liberty and then names two limits — usefulness, and mastery. A thing may be permitted and still unwise, and it may be permitted and still enslaving. Paul also uses the word to claim a civil right: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?” (Acts 22:25), which shows a Christian may lawfully appeal to law.

Webster 1828 Definition

What is permitted — and never the last question. Christ asks whether it is lawful to do good on the sabbath; Paul grants that all things are lawful and adds two limits, expediency and mastery.

expand to see more

LAWFUL, a. Agreeable to law; conformable to law; allowed by law; legal; legitimate.

2. Constituted by law; rightful; as the lawful owner of lands.

3. LAWFULLY, adv. Legally; in accordance with law.

4. LAWFULNESS, n. The quality of being conformable to law; legality.

5. In Scripture, permitted; it is not lawful for thee to have her, Matt. 14; all things are lawful for me, 1 Cor. 6.

Key Scripture

Matthew 12:2 — "But when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto him, Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day."

Mark 3:4 — "And he saith unto them, Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill? But they held their peace."

1 Corinthians 6:12 — "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any."

Acts 22:25 — "And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?"

Modern Corruption

Christian liberty is treated as a verdict rather than a starting point — if a thing is lawful, no further question is asked — while the legalist asks only whether it is permitted and never whether it is good.

expand to see more

Two opposite parties both stop at the word lawful. The legalist asks what is permitted in order to draw a boundary and police it, and Matthew 12 shows where that ends: men able to identify a technical sabbath violation in hungry disciples, and unable to answer whether it is lawful to do good on the sabbath. Legalism is not an excess of seriousness about God's law; it is a substitution of a manageable rule for the law's actual intent. The antinomian asks the same question for the opposite reason — to establish that nothing forbids him — and treats a clean legal verdict as the end of the matter. Paul answers this second party directly, and it is worth noticing that he does not dispute the premise. He concedes all things are lawful and then says the concession settles less than they think.

The principle to recover is Paul's pair of tests. First, expediency: is this profitable, does it build up, does it serve anyone. Second, and sharper, mastery: I will not be brought under the power of any. A lawful thing that has begun to own a man has already answered the question, whatever the verdict on its lawfulness. This is a far more searching standard than a list of prohibitions, and it cannot be applied to a neighbour — only to oneself. Romans 14 adds the third consideration, the weaker brother, and between them these three settle nearly every question of Christian liberty without needing a new rule.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek exesti is the impersonal it is lawful, it is permitted. Hebrew has no exact equivalent; the Old Testament asks rather what is commanded or forbidden, which is itself instructive.

expand to see more

Greek exesti (G1832) — it is lawful, it is permitted; the word in every is it lawful question.

Greek sumphero (G4851) — to be profitable, expedient; Paul's first limit in 1 Corinthians 6:12.

Greek exousiazo (G1850) — to exercise authority over; brought under the power of any.

Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom; the standing the question presupposes.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, ordinance, what is right; the Old Testament's framing of the question.

Usage

"Of the Pharisees' first question: thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day (Matthew 12:2)."

"Of the question they could not answer: is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days (Mark 3:4)."

"Of liberty with two limits: all things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient (1 Corinthians 6:12)."
